en: For the sake of dispelling grief, one should speak a discourse such as this: "Toward a friend who is virtuous and affectionate, or even toward one's own dependent kin, when they have met with an inevitable fate, one should cast off sorrow because it is useless. (11.1)
For one who is not free from passion, grief surely comes upon the loss of a loved one like a great flood; yet the wise man should not be deluded by it. 11.2
For what acquisition of merit would come to him from that, or what benefit to his own self, regarding friends who share in his joys and sorrows or his kinsmen? (11.3)
A wise man should not indulge in grief; rather, he should strive for its cessation through discernment.
For who indeed would resort to an object that destroys one's virtues and whose very nature is devoid of happiness? (11.4)

But how is this grief said to strike down one's virtues? This is not to be understood through mere explanation, for it is evident to direct perception. For a person who persists in the darkness of grief, the splendor of his fortitude is withdrawn; the capacity of his intellect is closed; the prowess of his memory is cut away; his inner heat (tejas) becomes extinguished; his vigor abandons him; joy does not approach him; and the clarity of his mind recedes far from him.

Even in matters concerning righteousness, wealth, fame, or patience, his enthusiasm utterly falters. His clarity fades away. Due to mental agitation, his health falls into a state of flux from failing to take food and other necessities at the proper time. His radiance becomes as if beset by calamity. The brilliance that crushes the darkness of enemies withers, and his strength dissolves. Fortune becomes distressed; his regard for courtesy, discipline, and respect grows lax; and his acuity succumbs to emaciation.

Good cheer comes to an end, and happiness becomes difficult to sustain; such is sorrow, which strikes down the side of virtue. Therefore, for one whose soul is fond of virtue and whose mind is ever intent on its preservation, it is not fitting to follow that sorrow which obstructs the side of virtue.
Thus, it is well for you to adopt that very same designation.
"Even if this enemy, grief, has taken root within these [faculties] that end with the mind, it is indeed an obstructor of virtue; it must not be thus neglected by those such as you. (11.5)
When the virtues of the virtuous have been nurtured until they bear fruit and have become their very nature,
what indeed could grief do, even if it were to descend upon them?
But an offense against one's virtues must not be tolerated. || 11.6 ||
Elsewhere, they do not wish for grief— which is a foe to the side of virtue— to expand;
yet they treat that [grief] with utter contempt when it reaches the heights of the mind.
But once it has been attained, what wise person here could endure it? || 11.7 ||
There is much to be reflected upon that is joined with dharma and purpose, as well as duties that bring about fame and happiness;
direct your mind toward those very things.
For those such as you, infamy is indeed sorrow. || 11.8 ||
This is indeed a street of base people trodden by those of little spirit; for,
without investigating the stability of the world— which is as flickering as the moon reflected in water— they maintain it with meager qualities of fortitude.
Moreover, when their beloveds pass away, people have their splendor robbed by the misery of vast grief. || 11.9 ||
Yet, even though hidden by profundity, the glory of a virtuous person's qualities then comes to light;
just as this happens, how could misfortune ever approach?
And yet, how is it that grief still comes upon me? 11.10
Finding no opportunity for lamentation due to their steadfast nature,
yet expressing themselves through thoughts following from their grateful disposition,
they had cast off their ornaments in conformity with worldly custom, as is the way of the wise.
Faces shine when their beloveds are in distress; one's own virtues adorn them. || 11.11 ||

Even disregarding compassion for their own lives, virtuous men pursue only excellence and do not yield to the side of vice; therefore, you ought to summon fortitude to withstand this overwhelming grief and despondency. Let your memory be steadied in your mind, lest it depart under the sway of anger; let your brilliance be directed toward the support of sacred learning, and let your intellect be awakened by reflecting upon that [learning].

For in which branch of knowledge has the persistence of grief ever been sanctioned by any author of a treatise? Therefore, let the lamp of wisdom be kindled—it which dispels the darkness of sorrow and reveals the true nature of the world’s condition.
Even in the triple heaven there is no eternal stability; even after exercising the sovereignty of great Indra, they fall from the celestial realm.
Due to the exhaustion of the fruit of their meditative absorption,
thousands of the hosts of Brahmās fall helplessly downward.
The Ābhāsvara gods, whose forms are radiant,
and the Śubha gods, who possess beautiful and auspicious forms,
as well as those higher than them, have not yet seen the Truths.
Those whose splendor has fallen away undergo ruin. || 11.13 ||
Even those gods who live for many thousands of eons, who are formless, and who have reached the peak of existence,
[must fall] due to the exhaustion of their own performed merit.
Thereupon, inauspicious states of existence come to an end. || 11.14 ||
Thus, even the deities, having long enjoyed various pleasures based upon their own past deeds,
fall helplessly from heaven.
Therefore, there is no state of refuge within the realms of existence. || 11.15 ||

Even in heaven, birth is thus accompanied by suffering, involving the hardships of disease, exertion, and affliction; among humans it is likewise so, whereas in the miserable realms (apāya), there is nothing but pure suffering. Therefore—
One should know that birth is the foundation of all suffering. || 11.16 ||
It does not exist, yet the arising of suffering is not absent; for when the mind is absent, how can there be the occurrence of mental factors? And the body, which causes affliction, has come to rest.
How, then, could there be suffering which has that as its basis? (11.17)
As long as the mind remains deluded by the conceptualization of relishing [sensual] flavors, it yearns for rebirth;
so long does the process of suffering continue.
Thirst is severed and suffering has vanished. || 11.18 ||
Seeing that these things are essence-less, perishable, linked with suffering, and devoid of self,
you abandon craving; and through the disappearance of that craving, [you attain liberation].
There is no further recurrence of suffering whatsoever. || 11.19 ||
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying this sorrow, lamentation, and the suffering of birth and so forth,
follow the path trodden by the noble beings.
For there is no limit of place or time for the persistence of sorrow.
For thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"O monks, [this path] is the one-way path found by me.
Therefore, having obtained a birth among humans, which is so difficult to attain...

And practice the Sugata’s word which leads to the destruction of suffering; exert yourself for the attainment of your own welfare in such a way that this kind of misery may never be yours again. (11.21)

"For the convergence of the moment for attaining the highest good is indeed extremely rare; therefore, those who desire their own welfare do not fall into negligence. Regarding this, after stating the illustration of the door-panel and the wall as they are traditionally heard, it should be said:
"Having thus observed this extreme rarity of the moment for attaining the highest good, devote yourself solely to that which is beneficial and abandon useless grief. (11.22)
Another interpretation:
[wealth] has meager gain, is touched by the fruit of suffering, entails great ruin, and is an adversary to dharma and fame.
The virtuous do not desire to attain such a thing as this; for who would resort to such misfortune? (11.23)
But grief is an enemy that obstructs the performance of duty; it results in either diminished success or a total lack of success.
Therefore, sharpness of mind arising at the proper time is essential for action.
For when employed in her duties, she will bring about prosperity. || 11.24 ||

And how could that sequence exist for one whose mind is distracted by the darkness of grief, who is overwhelmed by dejection, and whose memory is impaired by despondency? Therefore, since grief has a meager arising or no arising at all, it should not be pursued. Furthermore, because it increases the torment of the mind, the fire of grief touches upon the fruit of suffering.
How can there be happiness when the mind is tormented, given that the physical body is its very support? (11.25)

Thus, grief—which consists of the very nature of suffering and involves the touch of the fruit of suffering—is itself of the essence of pain. And because its flow is not restrained due to a lack of analytical discernment (*apratisaṃkhyāna*), it gains strength through recurrence and, being nourished, it violently destroys the splendor of fortitude, overcomes mindfulness, and agitates the bodily constituents such as wind (*anila*) and the others. It then gives rise to a mental affliction or some other disorder that obstructs life-force, manifesting as a disease or a crisis. Therefore, because it results in such great calamity, grief is simply not fit for persistence.
Moreover, because it stands as an adversary to the fame of the Dharma, sorrow must be utterly shunned from afar;
for how can there be the steadfastness required for the practice of Dharma in those whose minds are dulled by despondency and dejection caused by grief?
And for one deprived of her, what is the state of being human? For his perceptions regarding dharma are equal to those of beasts and the like. || 11.26 ||
One should not direct grief toward this [body] from one's own mind, for in that way there would be a neglect of the Dharma;
it is of greater benefit even than toward one's dearest friends.
What wise person indeed would disparage the Dharma? || 11.27 ||
Who indeed that is wise would fail to attain fame, knowing that by violating righteousness and following grief, one brings about unhappiness both in this world and in the next?
By means of strength, one should abandon that very [lack of fortitude]. || 11.28 ||
Thus, cast away well this wretchedness of grief from your mind, which is an enemy to your fame for dharma—
like one whose eyes are blurred by tears through unrighteousness.
Why do you undergo exhaustion on a path that is not the way? 11.29
When a calamity has arrived, what rule that does not serve as its remedy—what wise man would pursue such a thing, which is nothing but the fruit of his own toil? (11.30)

Therefore, summoning fortitude and applying mindfulness to the practice of following what you have heard, open wide the eye of wisdom by reflecting upon the nature of the world; you ought to abandon in every way this wretchedness of grief, which is unfit for one who has renounced all attachments.
Let the long-lived one observe:

if this man, like a traveler, has come from somewhere and, having stayed near you for a moment as if from the fatigue of the road, has now departed for elsewhere—what is the use of persisting in grief over that? This is simply the nature of travelers.

If you have been made affectionate toward him by the emergence of his virtues, yet you consider this cleverness of his for his own sake to be due to his extreme nobility—who indeed would feel affection for a person consumed by a lack of virtue?

And if he does not perceive this state of yours born of grief, or if, being under the sway of agitation, shame, and torment, he knows it but does not grant his command—then having transgressed even Yama himself, how can he still be considered affectionate?

But if this [course] is simply not possible, then what is the point of distressing people whose suffering and joy are equal to one's own with grief and dejection? Whatever must be done next by the Noble One—that is what should be done; such is the proper course.
Therefore, cast off this grief from your mind; this is not the time for sorrow, for this is the time that urges people toward the practice of the true nature of Dharma.
Be vigilant in every duty that is certain to bring about your own welfare.
Let the activity of your mind be directed toward the establishment of the realization of reality.
Having understood the irresistible power of death, observed the fickle nature of life, and recognized that there is no remedy for grief in that regard,
[one should act].
A wise person should strive for their own welfare alone. || 11.33 ||

Furthermore, that benefit for oneself, when being practiced, is accomplished through reliance upon the three bases of meritorious action; it is mundane. As was said by the Blessed One, having spoken the sūtra: "These three... [the remainder] should be recited.
In that regard, giving accomplishes many virtues; therefore, it is for one's own benefit. For example, it should be said: "The radiance of knowledge."
Likewise regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*), as it has been said:
"From family, from wealth, and from ornaments...
Likewise, regarding cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it has been stated that it brings about rebirth in the Brahma-world and so forth.

Thus, observing *saṃsāra* as a thicket crowded with the thorns of manifold calamities and desiring the cessation of all suffering, one should meditate for the sake of seeing the Four Noble Truths. As it was said by the Blessed One:
"O monks, those who understand this suffering as it truly is do not go to hell," and so forth.
In this regard, one should speak after first providing the preceding exposition.
Having seen the noble truths exactly as they are,
one no longer undergoes the suffering of a miserable rebirth;
for those faults which serve as the causes for an evil destiny [are thereby abandoned].
The seer of truth abandons them all. || 11.34 ||
Then, having dispelled other forms of darkness through meditative cultivation, just as the sun does with its radiance,
he no longer falls under the power of suffering.
And he attains the supreme bliss of Nirvana. || 11.35 ||

Thus, perceiving these unpleasant things to be impermanent, unstable, and lacking in ultimate duration, one should cultivate only a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in the mind. For one whose heart is agitated by grief is not fit for the task of practicing what is beneficial. In this regard, after recounting the *Ayogṛha-jātaka* as it is heard in tradition, it should be said:
"Having thus observed that [the world] is ablaze on all sides by the fire of Death, whose vigor is irresistible—"
Seeing the world wailing, protectorless, and afflicted, the wise man should tread the path of spiritual urgency for the sake of peace. 11.36

Another interpretation: A wise person, recollecting the unimpeded knowledge of the Buddhas everywhere and their supreme desire for the welfare of others, should not harbor pride regarding their word. (11.37)
Even one endowed with knowledge, if not engaged in what is beneficial,
would not be wise even if striving for the good;
therefore, one should not act upon the words of either without careful examination.
How much more so for one who would be devoid of both of them. || 11.38 ||
But for him whose intellect regarding all objects of knowledge functions in the world with a disposition toward the welfare [of others],
the activity of his speech proceeds unimpeded.
What is the purpose of undergoing the exhaustion of deliberation? || 11.39 ||

And the disciples, whose minds were agitated by the persistence of their grief, were turned away by the Blessed One from that sorrow which brings about the consequence of continued suffering and dejection, which is useless, and which robs one of virtues.
Just as in the case of the elder woman Urvarī, who was afflicted by grief for her daughter, as it has been said: "O mother, live! O mother, live! you cry out.
Likewise, the elderly woman Vāsiṣṭhī, whose heart was tormented by the dart of grief for her son, was turned back from that sorrow for her son. As it is said:
"He whose path you do not know, whether he has come or gone...

Similarly, King Prasenajit, afflicted by grief for his mother, established himself through the recollection of the Tathāgata’s words; and by the Blessed One’s permission regarding that course of action and by demonstrating the meaning of that matter in detail, he was turned away from the persistence of his grief. As it is said:
The sūtra should be recalled: "Venerable sir, my noble mother has passed away.
Likewise, the Elder Āryānanda, his mind overwhelmed by grief that the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, was restrained by the Blessed One from the persistence of his sorrow.
"Enough, Ānanda, do not grieve," and so forth.

Likewise, for the sake of extracting the thorn of various occasional griefs from sentient beings, the Blessed One, out of supreme compassion for others, taught five objects of focus (*ālambanīya*). By demonstrating these, the Elder Ārya Nārada rescued King Muṇḍa as he was sinking into the mire of grief caused by the death of his wife. As it has been said:
Having cited the Sūtra which says, "O Great King, these five are to be relied upon," one should speak thus regarding the fire of grief within the minds of those to be trained.
Though being stirred up by the winds of evil thoughts,
that foremost of sages did not neglect him; he brought him to calmness with the waters of his speech.
For how could a Sage overlook the growing misfortune in the hearts of others,
he who always regards all beings as his own children?
The supreme application of the resolute intention for the welfare [of others]. || 11.41 ||
And that most compassionate best of sages did not permit him to follow;
for who indeed would allow a wise man to fall into such a state?
One should not make grief devoid of an object for the mind. || 11.42 ||
What, then, is the means for that? It is said:
having recognized this outflow of what is dear, one should not fixate upon attachment toward it.
Observing the defect of the nature of the world's activity, which is exceedingly fickle. || 11.43 ||
For thus it was said by the Blessed One in these two verses beginning with: "Whatever sorrows or lamentations there may be..."
The three verses beginning with "Suffering arises from what is dear," and likewise:
"O village headman, for whom there are four things dear, for him there are four sufferings."
And as it has been said:
"O Nāgila, this excrement and urine—which is the result of what was eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—is [the outcome] of that which is desired and beloved.
Therefore it is said:"

That which is bitter with grief, exhaustion, despondency, and wretchedness during separation from what is dear is therefore unpleasant to those who possess self-mastery; hence, its avoidance is pleasant for them.
But for the foolish, whose minds are as restless as moths and who look only for immediate gratification, it is otherwise.
In the same way, even when presenting that which is born of what is unpleasant, one does not [actually] present anything unpleasant or disagreeable. 11.44.

Moreover, having understood that such suffering, beginning with grief, has its cause in what is dear, one should not wander into the attachment of affection for it. Furthermore, because they are unstable by nature, things that are pleasant for only a moment—
When there is much suffering at the time of separation, who indeed would set their heart upon the company of loved ones, which is like a dream? (11.45)
As it was said by the Supreme Sage in two verses beginning with: "Just as in a dream, there is a meeting... and so forth.
And as for that remedy which has neither existed in the past nor will exist in the future—what person, in such a calamity, ought to follow it? (11.46)
Therefore, relying on that fortitude, abandon your grief;
for this is truly not the path for one such as you, who are discerning and self-possessed.
Lack of fortitude is as unbecoming [in him] as it would be in a mountain. || 11.47 ||
To him who was thus engaged in this extensive suffering of birth,
he spoke the Dharma for its transcendence.
Therefore, for the destruction of that grief, remember the Jina.
As it has been said:
"Thus indeed is that Blessed One"—
in this way, the recollection of the qualities of the Sage brings forth joy.
It performs the cause for the accomplishment of the accumulation of merit;
therefore, by it, the darkness of grief is dispelled, just as darkness is dispelled by the radiance of the thousand-rayed sun.
And at the end of the day, darkness, struck down by the radiance of the sun, expands once more;
yet that which has been uprooted by the cultivation of mindfulness of the Sage’s virtues does not return.
The darkness of grief is not born again and again. || 11.50 ||
As it has been said:
"And these, monks, are the recollections. Therefore, O gentle one, having established mindfulness upon the qualities of the Victor, [proceed].
Abandon grief, the root of vast exhaustion and suffering; look upon your devoted people, your own kin, and your friends as those whose joys and sorrows are one with yours through affection.
Just as Rāhu, yawning while the sun is shining, throws the world into utter confusion, so does the darkness of grief, resting upon the consciousness, throw people into turmoil.
Therefore, you ought not to tolerate this. || 11.52 ||
Just as a fire spreading at the peak of a house, or a disease that has entered the body,
or a venomous serpent being overlooked within one's home.
Therefore, this grief should not be pursued in the mind. || 11.53 ||
And as for what is meaningless, a wise person should not indulge in it for long; for even after weeping, what benefit could there be?
One should do so only by taking into account such as the nature of the world.
One’s mind should be directed toward the path of liberation. || 11.54 ||
As it has been said:
"The single path is to be investigated."
